title:
Ma Teng raises an army to aid the royal house
Cao Cao goes to war to avenge his father
paragraphs:
Now the two traitors [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) meant to murder [Emperor Xian](char-prince-xie), but [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) spoke against it: "It will not do. If we kill him today, men may not submit to us. Better to go on serving him as our sovereign, lure the lords in through the passes, and clip his wings first. Then we can kill him, and the realm will be ours for the taking." Li Jue and Guo Si took their advice and put up their swords. [The Emperor](char-prince-xie) called down from the tower: "[Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) has been put to death. Why have you not drawn off your men?" Li Jue and Guo Si said: "We have done the royal house good service but have been given no rank for it, so we dare not withdraw." The Emperor said: "What ranks would you have?"
[Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) each wrote out the titles he wanted and sent them up, and [the Emperor](char-prince-xie) could only comply. Li Jue was made General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis of Chiyang, with the office of Director of Retainers and [the staff and axe](misc-staff-and-axe). Guo Si was made General of the Rear, with the staff and axe as well, and the two were to hold the government of the court together. Fan Chou became General of the Right and Marquis of Wannian, and Zhang Ji General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Pingyang, with his troops stationed at [Hongnong](loc-hongnong). The rest, [Li Meng](char-li-meng) and [Wang Fang](char-wang-fang) among them, were each made a Colonel. Then they thanked the Emperor for his grace and led their troops out of the city. They gave orders besides to search for [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s remains, and some scraps of skin and bone were found. These were fitted into a body carved of fragrant wood, great funeral rites were held, and it was given the robes, cap and double coffin of a prince and carried on a chosen lucky day to [Meiwu](loc-meiwu) for burial. But when the hour came a great thunderstorm broke, the water lay several chi deep on level ground, and a thunderbolt split the coffin and flung the body out. Li Jue waited for clear weather and buried it again, yet that night the same thing happened. Three times they tried a new grave and could not bury it, until the lightning had consumed the last scrap of his skin and bone. Great indeed was Heaven's anger against Dong Zhuo!
Now that [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) held supreme power, they oppressed the people cruelly and secretly set trusted men of their own about [Emperor Xian](char-prince-xie) to watch his movements, so that he moved as though among thorns at every step. The officers of the court rose and fell at the two traitors' pleasure. To win men's good opinion they summoned [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) to court, made him Minister Coachman, and gave him a share in the government. One day word came that [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng), Grand Administrator of [Xiliang](loc-xiliang), and [Han Sui](char-han-sui), Inspector of [Bing Province](loc-bing-province), were bearing down on [Chang'an](loc-changan) with more than a hundred thousand men, declaring that they came to punish the traitors. The two generals had in fact sent men into Chang'an beforehand and leagued themselves with three who were to act for them within the city, Ma Yu the Palace Attendant, Chong Shao the Counselor Remonstrant and Liu Fan the Left General of the Household, to plot together against the traitors' party. The three had secretly memorialized [the Emperor](char-prince-xie), who made Ma Teng General of the Western Campaign and Han Sui General of the Western Garrison, and each had received a secret edict to join forces and punish the traitors.
When [Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) heard that the two armies were at hand, they met to decide how to resist them. The counselor [Jia Xu](char-jia-xu) said: "The two armies have come a long way. The only course is to keep behind deep ditches and high walls and hold fast against them. Within a hundred days their grain will be spent and they will have to draw off. Then lead your men after them, and you will take both generals." [Li Meng](char-li-meng) and [Wang Fang](char-wang-fang) stepped forward. "That is a poor plan. Lend us ten thousand picked men, and we will have the heads off [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng) and [Han Sui](char-han-sui) at once and lay them at your feet." Jia Xu said: "If you fight now you are sure to be beaten." Li Meng and Wang Fang cried with one voice: "If we two are beaten, you may have our heads, but if we win, you must forfeit yours to us." Jia Xu said to Li Jue and Guo Si: "Two hundred li west of [Chang'an](loc-changan) lie the Zhouzhi hills, where the road is steep and dangerous. Let Generals Zhang Ji and Fan Chou camp there and hold it behind strong walls. Then Li Meng and Wang Fang may be left to take their own men and meet the enemy." Li Jue and Guo Si did as he said and gave Li Meng and Wang Fang fifteen thousand horse and foot. The two went off in high spirits and made their camp two hundred and eighty li from Chang'an. When the [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) troops came up, the pair led their men out to meet them. The Xiliang army drew up in line of battle across the road, and Ma Teng and Han Sui rode out side by side, pointed at Li Meng and Wang Fang and reviled them: "Traitors to the state! Who will go and take them?"
Before the words were out a young general came flying from the line, his face like jade in a cap and his eyes like shooting stars, with a tiger's body and an ape's arms, a panther's belly and a wolf's loins, a long spear in his hand and a fine horse under him. This was [Ma Chao](char-ma-chao), [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng)'s son, styled Mengqi, just seventeen years old and matchless in valor. [Wang Fang](char-wang-fang), thinking little of so young an opponent, put his horse forward to meet him. They had not fought many bouts when Ma Chao ran him through and he fell from his horse. Ma Chao turned his horse and was riding back when [Li Meng](char-li-meng), seeing Wang Fang killed, came galloping alone behind him. Ma Chao pretended not to notice. Ma Teng shouted from under the standard: "There is a man coming up behind you!"
The shout had not died away when [Ma Chao](char-ma-chao) was seen with [Li Meng](char-li-meng) a prisoner across his saddle. He had known well that Li Meng was after him and had loitered on purpose. When the horse drew close and the spear came thrusting at him he swayed aside, so that Li Meng lunged at empty air, and as the two horses came level Ma Chao stretched out his long arm and took him alive out of the saddle. The soldiers, with no one left to lead them, fled at the sight. [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng) and [Han Sui](char-han-sui) pressed the pursuit and won a great victory. They drove on to the mouth of the pass, camped there, and had Li Meng beheaded and his head set up as a warning.
When [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) learned that [Ma Chao](char-ma-chao) had killed both [Li Meng](char-li-meng) and [Wang Fang](char-wang-fang), they believed at last in [Jia Xu](char-jia-xu)'s foresight. They kept to his plan now and thought only of holding the pass, letting the enemy challenge as he would and never going out to meet him. Sure enough, in less than two months the [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) army was short of grain and fodder alike, and its leaders were debating a retreat. Just then a servant of Ma Yu's household in [Chang'an](loc-changan) informed against his master, and against Liu Fan and Chong Shao with him, for being in league with [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng) and [Han Sui](char-han-sui) outside and meaning to act for them within the city. Li Jue and Guo Si were furious. They seized every soul of the three households, old and young, master and servant, and beheaded them in the market place, and the heads of the three men were brought straight to the front and set up before the gate.
[Ma Teng](char-ma-teng) and [Han Sui](char-han-sui), with their grain spent and their plot within the city betrayed, could do nothing but break camp and retreat. [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) sent [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) with an army after Ma Teng and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) with another after Han Sui, and the [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) army was routed. [Ma Chao](char-ma-chao) fought desperately in the rear and beat Zhang Ji back. Fan Chou went after Han Sui and had all but overtaken him near [Chencang](loc-chencang), when Han Sui reined in and said to him: "You and I are men of the same district. Why so merciless today?" Fan Chou reined in too and answered: "I am under orders and may not disobey!" Han Sui said: "I came here for the state's sake as well. Why must you press me so hard?" At that Fan Chou turned his horse, called in his men and went back to camp, and let Han Sui go. But he had not counted on Li Bie, Li Jue's nephew, who saw him let Han Sui escape and went back to tell his uncle. Li Jue, in a great rage, was for marching against Fan Chou at once. [Jia Xu](char-jia-xu) said: "Men's minds are not yet settled, and to be forever taking up arms would be most unwise. Better lay a feast and invite Zhang Ji and Fan Chou to celebrate the victory, then seize Fan Chou at the table and behead him. Nothing could be easier."
[Li Jue](char-li-jue) was delighted. He laid the feast and invited [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou), and the two generals came to it gladly. Halfway through the feast Li Jue suddenly turned grim. "Fan Chou, why have you been dealing with [Han Sui](char-han-sui) and plotting rebellion?" Fan Chou was thunderstruck, and before he could answer men with swords and axes rushed out and struck off his head at the foot of the table. Zhang Ji fell on his face in terror. Li Jue raised him up and said: "Fan Chou plotted rebellion, and so I had him put to death. You are my own trusted friend. What have you to fear?" He put Fan Chou's troops under Zhang Ji's command, and Zhang Ji went back to [Hongnong](loc-hongnong).
After [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) had beaten the [Xiliang](loc-xiliang) troops, not one of the lords dared call them to account. [Jia Xu](char-jia-xu) urged them again and again to give the people peace and to make friends of men of worth and standing, and from this time the court showed some faint signs of life. Then, unlooked for, the Yellow Turbans of [Qing Province](loc-qing-province) rose again, some hundreds of thousands of them in bands under many chiefs, plundering honest folk. [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), the Minister Coachman, offered to recommend a man who could put the rebels down, and Li Jue and Guo Si asked who it was. Zhu Jun said: "If the rebels of [Shandong](loc-shandong) are to be broken, it must be [Cao Mengde](char-cao-cao) and no other." Li Jue said: "Where is Mengde now?" Zhu Jun said: "He is Grand Administrator of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery), and has a large force under him. Order him against the rebels, and they will be crushed in a matter of days." Li Jue was well pleased. He had an edict drafted that same night and sent a man with it to Dong Commandery, ordering [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) to join [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Chancellor of Jibei, against them. Cao Cao received the edict and joined forces with Bao Xin, and together they marched and struck the rebels at Shouyang. Bao Xin cut his way too deep into their ground and was killed. Cao Cao chased them as far as Jibei, where tens of thousands surrendered. He put the surrendered men in his van, and wherever his army came none failed to submit. In little more than a hundred days he had taken in over three hundred thousand soldiers who gave themselves up, with more than a million men and women besides. He picked out the best of them and named them the Qing Province troops, and the rest he sent back to their farms. From this time Cao Cao's name carried more weight by the day. When the report of the victory reached [Chang'an](loc-changan), the court raised him to General of the Eastern Garrison.
In [Yan Province](loc-yan-province) [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) set about drawing worthy and able men to him. An uncle and a nephew came to join him. The uncle was a man of Yingyin in [Yingchuan](loc-yingchuan), [Xun Yu](char-xun-yu) by name, Wenruo by style, and the son of Xun Kun. He had served [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and now left him for Cao Cao, who talked with him, was greatly pleased, and said: "This is my [Zifang](char-zhang-liang-zifang)!" And he made him a Major on his staff. The nephew, [Xun You](char-xun-you), styled Gongda, was a scholar known throughout the realm, who had once been a Gentleman of the [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate) and afterwards gave up his office and went home. Now he came with his uncle, and Cao Cao made him instructor to the army. Xun Yu said: "I have heard of a worthy man in Yan Province, but I do not know where he is now." Cao Cao asked who it was, and Xun Yu said: "A man of Dong'e in [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery), [Cheng Yu](char-cheng-yu) by name, styled Zhongde." Cao Cao said: "I too have long known him by name." He sent men to ask after him in his own district, and they found that he was studying in the hills. Cao Cao invited him with all courtesy, and when Cheng Yu came Cao Cao was overjoyed.
[Cheng Yu](char-cheng-yu) said to [Xun Yu](char-xun-yu): "I am an ignorant man who has seen little, and do not deserve your recommendation. But there is a man of your own district, [Guo Jia](char-guo-jia) by name, styled Fengxiao, who is one of the worthies of the age. Why not bring him in?" Xun Yu started. "I had almost forgotten him!" So he spoke to [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), who invited Guo Jia to [Yan Province](loc-yan-province), and they discussed the affairs of the realm together. Guo Jia recommended a descendant of [Emperor Guangwu](char-emperor-guangwu) in the direct line, a man of Chengde in [Huainan](loc-huainan), [Liu Ye](char-liu-ye) by name, styled Ziyang, and Cao Cao sent for him at once. Liu Ye in turn recommended two men: one of Changyi in Shanyang, [Man Chong](char-man-chong) by name, styled Boning, and one of Wucheng, [Lü Qian](char-lu-qian) by name, styled Zike. Cao Cao had long known both by reputation, and took them as Assistant Officers in his army. Man Chong and Lü Qian together recommended a man of Pingqiu in [Chenliu](loc-chenliu), [Mao Jie](char-mao-jie) by name, styled Xiaoxian, and Cao Cao made him an Assistant Officer too. A commander also came to join Cao Cao with several hundred men, a man of Juping in Taishan, [Yu Jin](char-yu-jin) by name, styled Wenze. Cao Cao saw that he was practiced with bow and horse and of uncommon skill at arms, and gave him a Major's command.
One day [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun) brought in a huge fellow to see [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). Asked who he was, Xiahou Dun said: "This is a man of [Chenliu](loc-chenliu), [Dian Wei](char-dian-wei) by name, stronger and bolder than other men. He followed [Zhang Miao](char-zhang-miao) once, but fell out with the men of his camp, killed some dozens of them with his own hand, and fled into the hills. I was out hunting when I saw him chase a deer across a mountain stream, and so I took him into my troop. I have brought him here to recommend him to you." Cao Cao said: "I can see from his great frame that he must be strong." Xiahou Dun said: "He once killed a man to avenge a friend and walked straight out through the crowded market with the head in his hand, and of some hundreds of people not one dared go near him. The pair of iron halberds he uses now weigh eighty jin, and he mounts with them under his arms and swings them as if they weighed nothing." Cao Cao bade Dian Wei show his skill there and then. Dian Wei took the halberds under his arms and galloped up and down. Just then the great banner before the tent was caught by the wind and rocked as if it must fall, and a crowd of soldiers could not hold it steady. Dian Wei got down from his horse, shouted them back, gripped the staff in one hand, and stood towering in the wind without stirring. Cao Cao said: "Here is [Elai](char-elai) of old!" He made him Commandant of the Guard, and took off the brocade coat he was wearing and gave it to him, with a fine horse and a carved saddle. From this time Cao Cao had wise counselors on the civil side and fierce generals on the military, and his might overawed [Shandong](loc-shandong). He then sent [Ying Shao](char-ying-shao), Grand Administrator of Taishan, to [Langya](loc-langya) Commandery to fetch his father [Cao Song](char-cao-song).
[Cao Song](char-cao-song) had left [Chenliu](loc-chenliu) to escape the troubles and was living in retirement at [Langya](loc-langya). On receiving the letter he set out at once for [Yan Province](loc-yan-province) with his younger brother Cao De and all his household, old and young, more than forty persons, with over a hundred attendants and as many carts. His road lay through [Xu Province](loc-xu-province), whose Grand Administrator, [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian), styled Gongzu, was a mild and kindly man, honest and sincere. He had long wished to make a friend of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) and had found no way to it. Learning now that Cao Cao's father was passing through, he went out to the border to meet him, bowed twice in respect, spread a great feast, and entertained him for two days. When Cao Song was ready to go on, Tao Qian saw him beyond the outer wall himself, and sent the Commandant [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai) with the five hundred men of his command to escort him.
[Cao Song](char-cao-song) and his household had come as far as the road between Hua and Fei when, at the turn of summer into autumn, a sudden heavy rain came on, and they had to seek a night's lodging in an old temple. The monks took them in. Cao Song settled his family and told [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai) to quarter his men in the two side galleries. The soldiers' clothes and gear were soaked through by the rain, and they were all grumbling. Zhang Kai called his headmen aside to a quiet place and said: "We were Yellow Turbans once. We gave ourselves up to [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian) because we had to, and have got nothing by it. Now here is Cao Song with baggage and carts past counting. Riches are within our grasp. Tonight at the third watch let us all cut our way in, kill Cao Song and his whole household, take the goods, and go off together to the hills as outlaws. What do you say to it?"
They all agreed. That night, with the wind and rain still unabated, [Cao Song](char-cao-song) was sitting up when a great shouting broke out on every side. Cao De took his sword and went out to look, and was run through. Cao Song hurried with one of his concubines round behind the abbot's quarters, meaning to climb the wall and escape, but she was too fat to get over it. In his panic he hid with her in the privy, and there the soldiers killed him in the tumult. [Ying Shao](char-ying-shao) barely escaped with his life and went off to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao). [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai) killed every one of Cao Song's household, took the goods, set fire to the temple, and fled with his five hundred men to [Huainan](loc-huainan). Later men made a poem on it:
> [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao), the treacherous hero all men praise,
> Slew the whole house of Lü in former days.
> Now all his kin by other men are killed;
> So Heaven's law repays, its round fulfilled.
Some of [Ying Shao](char-ying-shao)'s soldiers who had escaped with their lives brought the news to [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). When he heard it he fell to the ground weeping, and those about him raised him up. He ground his teeth and said: "[Tao Qian](char-tao-qian) loosed his soldiers to kill my father. He and I cannot both live under heaven! I will raise my whole army and lay [Xu Province](loc-xu-province) waste, and only then shall I be avenged!" He left [Xun Yu](char-xun-yu) and [Cheng Yu](char-cheng-yu) with thirty thousand men to hold the three counties of [Juancheng](loc-juancheng), Fan and Dong'e, and with all the rest came driving upon Xu Province. [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun), [Yu Jin](char-yu-jin) and [Dian Wei](char-dian-wei) led the van. Cao Cao gave orders that wherever a city was taken, every one of its people should be slaughtered in vengeance for his father. Bian Rang, the Grand Administrator of Jiujiang, was a close friend of Tao Qian's, and on hearing that Xu Province was in danger he came with five thousand men of his own to its relief. Cao Cao flew into a rage at the news, and sent Xiahou Dun to cut him off on the road and kill him.
At this time [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) was an Assistant Officer of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery), and he too was a close friend of [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian). Hearing that [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) had raised his army for vengeance and meant to kill all the people, he rode through the night to see him. Cao Cao knew that he came to plead for Tao Qian and would have refused, but he could not forget what he owed him, and so had him asked into the tent. Chen Gong said: "I hear, Your Excellency, that you are bringing a great army down on [Xu Province](loc-xu-province) to avenge your father, and mean to kill all the people wherever you go. I have come to offer a word of counsel. Tao Qian is a good and upright man, not the kind to put profit before honor. Your father's death was [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai)'s wickedness and no fault of Tao Qian's. And what wrong have the people of the province and its counties done you? No good can come of killing them. I beg you to think twice before you act." Cao Cao said angrily: "You cast me off once and went your way. How have you the face to come before me again? Tao Qian has killed my whole family, and I have sworn to tear out his gall and cut out his heart to slake my hatred! You may plead his cause all you like, but what can you do if I will not listen?" Chen Gong took his leave and went out, sighing: "Nor have I the face to go back to Tao Qian!" And he rode off to join [Zhang Miao](char-zhang-miao), Grand Administrator of [Chenliu](loc-chenliu).
Now wherever [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s great army came it slaughtered the people and dug up the graves. When [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian), in [Xu Province](loc-xu-province), heard that Cao Cao had raised his army for vengeance and was killing the people, he looked up to heaven and wept aloud: "I have offended against Heaven, and brought this great calamity on the people of Xu!" He gathered his officers in haste to take counsel. [Cao Bao](char-cao-bao) said: "Cao Cao's troops are upon us. Are we to fold our hands and wait for death? Let me help you break them, Your Lordship."
[Tao Qian](char-tao-qian) had no choice but to lead his troops out to meet the enemy. Seen from afar, [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s army lay like spread frost and drifted snow, and in its center stood two white banners written large with four characters, Vengeance and Redress. The two armies drew up in line of battle. Cao Cao rode out before his line dressed in the plain white of mourning, raised his whip and railed at him. Tao Qian rode out too beneath his standard, bowed from the saddle and said: "It was because I wished to win your friendship, Your Excellency, that I charged [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai) with the escort. I never thought he was still a robber at heart, and this is what came of it. Truly it was none of my doing, and I beg you to look into it." Cao Cao cursed him: "Old wretch! You killed my father, and you still dare talk nonsense! Who will take the old villain alive?" [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun) rode out at the word. Tao Qian fled back into his line in alarm, and Xiahou Dun was coming after him when [Cao Bao](char-cao-bao) leveled his spear and put his horse forward to meet him. The two horses had just closed when a wild wind sprang up, sand flew and stones rolled, both armies fell into disorder, and each side drew off its men.
[Tao Qian](char-tao-qian) went into the city and took counsel with his officers: "[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s force is too great to be withstood. I will bind myself and go to his camp and let him cut me to pieces as he will, to save the people of [Xu](loc-xu-province)." Before he had done speaking a man came forward and said: "Your Honor, you have long held Xu Province, and the people are grateful for your kindness. Cao Cao's troops are many, but they cannot break our city at a stroke. Hold fast with the people and do not go out. I have no great ability, but I have a small plan to offer that will leave Cao Cao without so much as a grave to lie in!" They were all astonished, and asked what the plan might be. Truly:
> He sought a friend and found a foe instead;
> Who knew that life would spring where hope lay dead?
Who this man was, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: Cao Song
versions.description: Father of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). Born of the Xiahou house and passed by adoption into the Cao family, as son of the eunuch Cao Teng.

versions.description: Father of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). Born of the Xiahou house and passed by adoption into the Cao family, as son of the eunuch Cao Teng. Killed with his whole household by [Zhang Kai](char-zhang-kai)'s soldiers.

versions.name: Dong Zhuo
versions.description: Chancellor of State and Grand Preceptor, who made himself master of the court. Cut down at the palace gate by his foster son [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu).

versions.name: Elai
